newsitem.title: CHINA: International labour slams China over protests.
newsitem.headline: International labour slams China over protests.

text.p: The international labour movement on Friday blasted China for breaking up worker protests this month, urging the need for freedom of association and collective bargaining in the communist nation.

Chinese police dispersed thousands of angry factory workers and arrested several of their leaders who staged noisy protests in Mianyang city in southwestern Sichuan province in early July after their employers declared bankruptcy.

In a statement received by fax, the Brussels-based ICFTU called on China to release those arrested in the Mianyang protests and to ensure that any workers injured in clashes with police received proper medical care.
"The ICFTU is also asking the government to ensure that the workers get the compensation and unemployment relief due to them under Chinese law," the statement said.
Local officials said thousands took to the streets on July 7 to protest against the closure of several state-owned enterprises. Several ringleaders were arrested, they said.

The ICFTU said it would file a complaint with the International Labour Office in Geneva if those arrested were not released. It urged Chinese authorities to resolve the crisis in Mianyang in accordance with international labour standards.
China's autocratic government had no standardised method for dealing with the concerns of workers, a shortcoming that only exacerbated its growing labour problems, the ICFTU said.
"A principle cause of problems like these is the lack of a fair system of industrial relations in China based on freedom of association and the promotion of collective bargaining," the ICFTU said.
Such a system would lay down proper procedures to resolve labour disputes, it said, voicing concern for China's methods.

"These moves are a step backward and coupled with the recent suspension of the new labour legislation in Hong Kong... sends a very worrying signal to the international community on future Chinese labour relations," the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU) said in a statement.

The Beijing-backed government of Hong Kong, which returned to Chinese rule on July 1 after 156 years as a British colony, on Wednesday suspended a set of labour laws, a move the ICFTU has slammed as trampling worker's rights.

Chinese officials have dismissed reports by Western human rights groups that 100,000 people were involved in the Mianyang protests and that paramilitary police used to break up the demonstrations had injured more than 100 people.

Worker unrest is one of the greatest fears of China's Communist Party leadership, still haunted by the international outrage that followed the bloody army crackdown on student-led pro-democracy demonstrations centred in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in June 1989.
Reports of increasing numbers of daring protests by disgruntled workers have surfaced in China in recent years as economic reforms have resulted in lay-offs from lumbering state factories.

China's leaders this year have placed reform of loss-making state enterprises at the top of their economic agenda, pushing through with bankruptcies that they had delayed for years for fear of social unrest.
